title: Illustration: Telling Stories with Pictures
summary: How illustrators draw pictures that go with written stories, how illustration differs from fine art, and how pictures have helped tell stories in books for a very long time.
poll: A picture can tell part of a story just as well as words can.

versions.title: Pictures That Tell Stories
versions.text:
Long ago and now, some books have pictures. They help tell the story. A worker makes each one. We call this worker an illustrator.

First, they read the story. Then they pick a scene. A scene can show a character.

They then draw it. The art shows what the words say.

Book art is not like wall art. Wall art can stand alone. It does not need words. Book art goes with the story.

Many books for kids have art like this. Each page can have one picture. It helps us see who is in the story.

Long ago, old books had art too. Workers drew it by hand. This was before new tools.

They plan their work with care. They pick shapes and colors that fit.

Good workers are still at work today. Art and words work well together.

versions.title: Pictures That Tell Stories
versions.text:
Long ago and now, many books have pictures in them. These pictures help tell the story. We call this kind of art an illustration. This worker is an illustrator.

First, they read the story closely. Next, they pick a part to draw. We call this part a scene. A scene can show a character. A character is just a person in the story.

Then they draw the scene by hand. The finished art shows what the words say.

A book picture is not quite like wall art. Wall art can stand alone. It does not need any words. A book picture goes with a story. It helps readers picture the story.

Many children's books use art this way. Each page can show one picture. The picture helps young readers see who is in the story. It also shows where it happens.

Long before new tools came along, old books had art too. Skilled workers drew these scenes by hand. They made one picture at a time.

They plan their work with great care. They choose shapes and colors that fit the story. The art must match the words.

Good workers are still at work today. They work closely with writers. Art and words work best together.

versions.title: Pictures That Tell Stories
versions.text:
Long ago and still today, many books use pictures along with words. These pictures help tell the story. We call this kind of picture an illustration. The person who makes one is an illustrator.

First, they read the story very closely. Next, they pick one part of the story to draw. We call this chosen part a scene. A scene often shows a main character. A character is simply a person in the story.

Then they draw that scene by hand. They try to match it closely to the words.

A book picture is not quite the same as wall art. A piece of wall art can stand on its own. It does not need any words at all. A book picture, though, is made to go with a story. It helps readers picture the story in their minds.

Many books made for children use pictures this way. Each page of a picture book can show one scene. The picture helps young readers see who is in the story and where it takes place.

Long before printing came along, old handwritten books had pictures too. Skilled workers drew these scenes by hand, one picture at a time, to help readers follow the story.

They always plan their work with great care. They choose shapes, lines, and colors that fit the story's mood. The finished picture must match the words, or readers may feel confused.

Skilled workers are still hard at work today. They work closely with writers to help bring a story to life. Pictures and words work best when they work well together.

versions.title: Pictures That Tell Stories
versions.text:
Long ago and still today, many books pair pictures with written words. These pictures help tell the story more fully than words alone. We call this kind of picture an illustration. The person who makes one is an illustrator.

First, they read the story closely, often more than once. Next, they pick one part of the story to draw. This moment matters to the plot. We call this part a scene. A scene often shows a main character. A character is simply a person or animal in the story.

Then they draw that scene by hand. They try to match it closely to the words on the page.

A book picture is not quite the same as wall art. A piece of wall art can usually stand on its own. It does not need any words at all. A book picture is made to go with a story. It helps readers picture the events more clearly.

Many books made for children rely on pictures in just this way. Each page of a picture book can show one scene. The picture helps young readers see who is in the story. It also shows where it happens and what is going on.

Long before printing came along, old handwritten books also included pictures. Skilled workers drew these story scenes by hand, one careful picture at a time, to help readers follow along.

They always plan their work with great care. They choose shapes, lines, and colors that fit the story's mood and meaning. The finished picture must match the words, or readers may end up feeling confused.

Skilled workers remain hard at work today, in books, magazines, and many other places. They work closely with writers to help bring a story to life, since pictures and words almost always work best when they work well together.

versions.title: Illustration: Telling Stories with Pictures
versions.text:
For as long as books have existed, many of them have paired pictures with written words. These pictures are called illustrations. They help tell a story more fully than words alone usually can. The person who creates one is called an illustrator.

An illustrator begins by reading a story very closely, often several times. Next, the illustrator chooses one meaningful moment from the story to draw. This chosen moment is called a scene. A scene often shows a character, a person or animal in the story.

The illustrator composes the scene with care. They decide what to depict. The picture must convey the story's mood to its audience in a vivid way.

Illustration is not quite the same thing as fine art. A piece of fine art can usually stand entirely on its own. It does not need any text to explain it. An illustration, by contrast, is made to accompany a story. It helps readers picture the events of a story more clearly in their minds.

Many books made for children rely heavily on illustration. Each page of a picture book might show one scene from the story. This helps young readers see who is in the story, where it takes place, and what is happening.

Long before printing presses existed, handwritten manuscripts also included illustrations. Skilled artists drew these story scenes by hand. Borders with patterns were often added too. This helped readers follow the tale as they read.

Illustrators plan their work with great care. They choose shapes, lines, and colors that fit the mood and meaning of the story. A picture that does not match its words can leave readers confused.

Skilled illustrators remain hard at work today, in books, magazines, and countless other places. They work closely alongside writers, because pictures and words usually tell a story best when they work together.

For as long as books have existed, many of them have paired pictures with written words, since illustrations can help tell a story more fully than words alone usually manage on their own.

An illustrator typically begins by reading a story very closely, often several times, to understand its characters, setting, and events. Next, the illustrator chooses one meaningful moment to draw, a moment known as a scene. The illustrator then renders that scene by hand, carefully matching it to the tone of the surrounding words.

The illustrator composes each scene with care, choosing a palette of colors and a stylized or realistic look that will complement the story's genre.

Illustration is not quite the same thing as fine art. A piece of fine art can usually stand entirely on its own, without needing any accompanying text to explain its meaning. An illustration, by contrast, is created specifically to accompany a narrative or another piece of writing, helping readers picture its events more vividly in their minds.

Many books made for children rely heavily on illustration, and each page of a picture book might depict one single scene, helping young readers see who is in the story, where it takes place, and what is happening at that moment.

Long before printing presses existed, handwritten manuscripts across many cultures also included illustrations. Skilled artists drew these story scenes by hand. Separate decorative borders were often added too. Artists carefully chose what to depict, never including anything considered improper for the audience of the time.

Illustrators plan their work with great care, deciding how to arrange each scene and which shapes, lines, and colors will best convey its mood. A picture that fails to match its surrounding words can easily leave readers confused rather than helped.

Skilled illustrators remain hard at work today, in books, magazines, and countless other places, working closely alongside authors, because pictures and words together usually convey a story more powerfully than either one manages alone.

versions.title: Illustration: Telling Stories with Pictures
versions.text:
For as long as books have existed, many of them have paired pictures with written words, since illustrations, as such pictures are known, can help convey a story more fully than words alone usually manage on their own, whatever the particular subject of that story happens to be, and an illustrator typically begins this demanding process by reading a story very closely, often several times, in order to understand its characters, setting, and events thoroughly before attempting to draw anything at all.

Next, the illustrator chooses one meaningful moment to depict, a moment known as a scene, and then renders that scene by hand with considerable skill, carefully matching it to the tone and pacing of the surrounding text, so that the finished picture feels like a natural, seamless extension of the writing itself rather than a separate, unrelated addition.

Illustration is not quite the same thing as fine art, even though the two fields clearly share a great many techniques and tools; a piece of fine art can usually stand entirely on its own, without needing any accompanying text whatsoever to explain its meaning, whereas an illustration is created specifically to accompany a narrative or another piece of writing, helping readers picture its unfolding events more vividly in their own minds as they read along.

Many books made for children rely heavily on illustration for exactly this reason, and each page of a picture book might depict one single scene, helping young readers see who is present in the story, where it takes place, and precisely what is happening at that particular moment in the unfolding plot, often before the young reader can decode every word on the page.

Long before printing presses existed anywhere in the world, handwritten manuscripts across many different cultures also included illustrations of this kind, and skilled artists drew these story scenes by hand, often alongside separate decorative borders, carefully choosing what to depict and deliberately never including anything considered improper for the audience of their own time and place.

Illustrators plan their work with great and sustained care, deciding how to compose each scene and choosing a palette of colors and a stylized or realistic look that will complement the story's genre and mood, since a picture that fails to match its surrounding words can all too easily leave readers feeling confused rather than genuinely helped.

Skilled illustrators remain hard at work today, in books, magazines, and countless other places, working closely alongside authors, because pictures and words together usually convey a story far more powerfully than either one manages entirely on its own, a creative partnership very nearly as old as the written word itself.

versions.title: Illustration: Telling Stories with Pictures
versions.text:
For as long as books have existed, a great many of them have paired carefully drawn pictures with written words, since illustrations, as such pictures are formally known, can help convey a story more fully and more memorably than words alone usually manage entirely unaided, whatever the particular subject of that story happens to be, and an illustrator typically begins this demanding process by reading a story with considerable attention, often several times over, in order to understand its characters, its setting, and its events thoroughly before attempting to draw anything at all, let alone a single finished scene.

Next, the illustrator chooses one meaningful moment to depict, a moment conventionally known as a scene, and then renders that scene by hand with considerable skill and patience, carefully matching it to the tone and pacing of the surrounding text, so that the finished picture feels like a natural, seamless extension of the writing itself rather than a separate, unrelated addition stitched awkwardly onto the page; illustration, in this sense, is not quite the same undertaking as fine art, even though the two fields clearly share a great many techniques, tools, and underlying skills, since a piece of fine art can usually stand entirely on its own, without needing any accompanying text whatsoever to explain or complete its meaning, whereas an illustration is created specifically and deliberately to accompany a narrative or another piece of writing, helping readers picture its unfolding events more vividly in their own imaginations as they read along.

Many books made for children rely heavily on illustration for precisely this reason, and each page of a picture book might depict one single scene, helping young readers see who is present in the story, where it takes place, and precisely what is happening at that particular moment in the unfolding plot, often well before the young reader is able to decode every single word on the page unaided.

Long before printing presses existed anywhere in the world, handwritten manuscripts across a great many different cultures also included illustrations of this very kind, and skilled artists drew these story scenes by hand, often alongside separate decorative borders, carefully choosing what to depict and deliberately never including anything considered improper for the audience of their own particular time and place.

Illustrators plan their work with great and sustained care, deciding how to compose each scene and choosing a palette of colors and a stylized or realistic look that will complement the story's genre and mood, since a picture that fails to match its surrounding words can all too easily leave readers feeling confused rather than genuinely helped along.

Skilled illustrators remain hard at work today, in books, magazines, and countless other places, working closely alongside authors, because pictures and words together usually convey a story far more powerfully than either one manages entirely on its own, a creative partnership very nearly as old as the written word itself and still thriving in classrooms and libraries everywhere.

wrong.C: Illustrators are shown planning their work with great care.

questions.stem: Why might old handwritten manuscripts have included illustrations?
options: Pictures helped readers follow the story as they read along
It replaced the need for any written words at all in the books
It made old manuscripts far heavier to carry around for the scribes
It helped hide the story from most curious readers who passed by
questions.why: The article says skilled artists drew scenes by hand to help readers follow the tale.

wrong.B: Illustrations accompanied words, not replaced them.
wrong.C: Weight is not discussed.
wrong.D: Illustrations helped readers, rather than hiding the story.

questions.stem: What can you infer about why children's books rely heavily on illustration?
options: Children's books never contain any written words at all
Illustrations always make books far more expensive to print
Pictures help young readers follow a story before reading every word
Publishers generally dislike using words in children's books
questions.why: The article explains pictures help young readers see who, where, and what is happening in a story.

wrong.A: Children's books are shown pairing pictures with written words.
wrong.B: Cost is not discussed in the article.
wrong.D: The article shows words and pictures working together, not publishers disliking words.

questions.stem: Why does the author explain the difference between illustration and fine art?
options: To argue that fine art is somehow not real art and should not be shown in museums
To help readers see what makes illustration its own kind of art
To prove that illustrators never study any fine art in school
To explain in some detail how old paper was made and why it turns yellow
questions.why: This comparison helps readers understand illustration's special purpose of accompanying a story.

wrong.A: The article does not dismiss fine art as not real.
wrong.C: The article does not discuss illustrators' training in fine art.
wrong.D: Papermaking is not discussed in this article.

MID.prompt: Explain how illustration is different from fine art, and why that difference matters for a children's book. Use the words depict and audience.
checklist: I explained the difference between illustration and fine art.
I explained why this difference matters for a children's book.
I used both key words correctly.
MID.modelAnswer: Fine art can stand completely on its own without any words, but illustration is made to depict a moment from a story so that it works together with the text. This difference matters for a children's book because its young audience often cannot yet read every word, so a picture that clearly depicts what is happening helps them follow the story anyway.

keyWords.definition: a story, or the way a story is told
keyWords.example: The documentary told its narrative through interviews and old photographs.

keyWords.definition: to go well with something and make it better or more complete
keyWords.example: The soft music complemented the quiet mood of the film.

keyWords.definition: the range of colors an artist chooses to use in a piece of work
keyWords.example: The painter used a warm palette of oranges and reds for the sunset scene.

keyWords.definition: drawn or shown in a particular artistic style rather than in a very realistic way
keyWords.example: The poster used stylized, simple shapes instead of detailed, realistic figures.

keyWords.definition: a category of art or writing that shares a similar style or subject
keyWords.example: Mystery is a popular genre of both books and films.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Printing presses were the very first tools used to create illustrations
Fine art and illustration are simply two names for one practice
Illustration only became important once children's books were invented
Illustrators create pictures that complement a narrative, distinct from fine art
questions.why: The article traces illustration's purpose, its distinction from fine art, and its long history before and after printing.

wrong.A: Handwritten manuscripts had illustrations before printing presses existed.
wrong.B: The article distinguishes the two practices clearly.
wrong.C: Manuscripts included illustrations long before children's books existed.

questions.stem: According to the article, what is a scene in illustration?
options: A chosen moment from a narrative that an illustrator renders by hand
A decorative border that is unrelated to the story itself, said the writer
A category of fine art that is unrelated to writing, said the writer
A tool once used to stretch leather tightly over boards, said the writer
questions.why: The article defines a scene as a meaningful moment an illustrator chooses to depict.

wrong.B: Borders are described as separate from the story scenes.
wrong.C: A scene relates specifically to illustration, not an unrelated category.
wrong.D: This describes bookbinding, a different craft.

questions.stem: How does the article distinguish illustration from fine art?
options: Fine art always depicts scenes, while illustration never does
Illustration needs no planning, while fine art needs careful composition
Fine art can stand alone, while illustration must accompany a narrative
Fine art is always more colorful than any illustration made
questions.why: The article explains fine art can stand alone, whereas illustration is created to accompany writing.

wrong.A: The article does not claim fine art always depicts scenes while illustration never does.
wrong.B: Illustrators are shown planning and composing their work carefully.
wrong.D: Color use is not compared this way in the article.

questions.stem: In the article, the word stylized most nearly describes pictures that are —
options: copied directly and exactly from an existing photograph
left completely blank and entirely unfinished
painted using only a single plain color
drawn in a particular style rather than very realistically
questions.why: The article uses stylized to describe pictures drawn in a particular artistic manner rather than a strictly realistic one.

wrong.A: Stylized is contrasted with photographic copying, not equated with it.
wrong.B: An unfinished picture is not what stylized describes.
wrong.C: Color count is unrelated to this meaning.

questions.stem: Why does the article say a picture that fails to match its surrounding text can leave readers confused?
options: Illustration is meant to complement and support the narrative around it
Fine art is always included in every illustrated storybook, so readers expect it
Illustrators never actually read the text before they draw their pictures
Children's books never contain any written narrative at all, only pictures
questions.why: The article explains illustration is created to accompany a narrative, so a mismatch undermines that purpose.

wrong.B: Fine art is distinguished from illustration, not included this way.
wrong.C: Illustrators are shown reading the story closely first.
wrong.D: Children's books are shown pairing illustration with written narrative.

questions.stem: What can you infer about why handwritten manuscripts across many cultures included illustrations?
options: Illustrations were only ever used within one single culture or one region
Readers across many cultures found pictures helped them follow a narrative
Old manuscripts never included any narrative to accompany
Illustrators refused to plan their careful work with any care
questions.why: The article says skilled artists across cultures drew scenes by hand to help readers follow the tale.

wrong.A: The article describes illustrations found across many different cultures, not just one.
wrong.C: Manuscripts are described as including both writing and illustrations.
wrong.D: Illustrators are described as planning their work with great care.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention that illustrators never included anything improper for their audience?
options: To highlight how illustrators considered their audience when choosing what to depict
To argue that illustrators ignored their own audience completely when they made pictures
To suggest illustration has no real connection to any narrative or story at all
To explain in detail how printing presses were first built in old workshops
questions.why: This detail shows illustrators thoughtfully considered their audience's expectations when choosing scenes.

wrong.B: The detail shows careful consideration, not disregard.
wrong.C: Illustration is tied closely to narrative throughout the article.
wrong.D: Printing presses are mentioned only briefly, not explained in depth.

questions.stem: How are composing a scene and choosing a palette related, according to the article?
options: Composing a scene replaces the need to choose any palette
A palette is chosen only after a book has already been printed
Both are choices an illustrator makes to convey a scene's mood
Composing a scene and choosing a palette are unrelated tasks
questions.why: The article describes illustrators composing scenes and choosing colors together to convey mood and meaning.

wrong.A: Composing a scene does not replace the need to also choose a palette.
wrong.B: These choices happen while creating the illustration, not after printing.
wrong.D: Both are described as central to an illustrator's planning, not unrelated.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how an illustrator uses composition and color choices to complement a narrative. Use the words palette and genre.
checklist: I explained how composition and color choices support a story.
I connected these choices to the idea of complementing a narrative.
I supported my answer with evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: An illustrator composes each scene carefully, deciding what to show and choosing a palette of colors that fits the story's mood, so the finished picture complements the narrative rather than distracting from it. Different genres often call for different choices, since a quiet, gentle story might use soft colors and simple shapes, while a more exciting narrative might use bolder lines and brighter colors to match its tone.

LOW.stem: What does the art in a kids' book help us see?
options: Where the book was made
Who is in the story
How long the book is
What the book costs
LOW.why: The text says the picture helps us see who is in the story.

wrong.A: The text does not say where the book was made.
wrong.C: The text does not talk about how long the book is.
wrong.D: The text does not talk about cost.

LOW.stem: Why can wall art stand alone?
options: It is always very large
It is made of stone
It has words on it
It does not need words
LOW.why: The text says wall art can stand alone because it does not need words.

wrong.A: The text does not say wall art is large.
wrong.B: The text does not say what wall art is made of.
wrong.C: The text says it does not need words.

LOW.stem: The text says wall art can stand alone. What does stand alone mean?
options: It needs no help
It is very tall and big
It has no color at all
It is far away from us
LOW.why: The next lines say wall art does not need words, so it needs nothing else.

wrong.B: The words are about needing words, not about height.
wrong.C: The text does not say wall art has no color.
wrong.D: The words are not about distance.

LOW.stem: Why must the shapes and colors fit the story?
options: So the book is much shorter
So art fits the words
So the pages are very bright
So the book can be sold fast
LOW.why: The text says the art shows what the words say, so it must fit the story.

wrong.A: The text does not say the art makes the book shorter.
wrong.C: Bright colors alone would not match the words.
wrong.D: The text does not talk about selling the book.

MID.stem: What might each page of a picture book show?
options: A map of the whole town
A long list of words
A scene from the story
The writer's full name
MID.why: The text says each page of a picture book might show one scene from the story.

wrong.A: The text does not say a page shows a map.
wrong.B: The pictures help tell the story with words.
wrong.D: The text does not say pages show the writer's name.

MID.stem: The text says the picture must convey the story's mood. What does convey mean?
options: Show or pass on
Hide or cover up
Cut or tear apart
Buy or sell it
MID.why: The picture must show the mood of the story to the audience in a vivid way.

wrong.B: The picture is meant to be seen.
wrong.C: The text does not talk about cutting a picture.
wrong.D: The text does not talk about buying or selling.

MID.stem: Why might an illustrator read a story several times before drawing?
options: To make the story longer
To find a printing press
To copy the words in the book
To know it very well
MID.why: The illustrator reads closely and then chooses one meaningful moment, so knowing the story well helps.

wrong.A: The illustrator does not change the story.
wrong.B: Printing presses are mentioned only for the past.
wrong.C: The illustrator draws pictures, not copies of words.

MID.stem: Why do illustrators work closely with writers today?
options: Pictures and words fit together
Writers cannot read the whole story
Illustrators never have any ideas
Books are only meant for writers
MID.why: The text says they work closely because pictures and words usually tell a story best when they work together.

wrong.B: Writers write the story, so they can read it.
wrong.C: Illustrators choose scenes and colors, so they have ideas.
wrong.D: The text says books use pictures and words.

HIGH.stem: The illustrator chooses colors that complement the story. What does complement mean here?
options: to go well with
to hide from
to argue against
to copy exactly
HIGH.why: The colors are chosen to suit the story's type and mood, so complement means to go well with.

wrong.B: The pictures support the story; they do not hide from it.
wrong.C: The art does not argue against the story.
wrong.D: The art adds to the story; it does not copy it.

HIGH.stem: What does an illustrator try to understand by reading a story closely?
options: Its characters, setting, and events
Its price and how many pages it has
Its printer and the year it was made
Its readers and where they live
HIGH.why: The article says the illustrator reads closely to understand characters, setting, and events.

wrong.B: Price and page count are not mentioned.
wrong.C: The article does not say the illustrator studies the printer.
wrong.D: The article does not say the illustrator studies where readers live.

HIGH.stem: What does the last paragraph suggest about illustration today?
options: It is no longer needed
It is still used in many places
It is only found in old books
It is done without authors
HIGH.why: The paragraph says illustrators remain at work in books, magazines, and countless other places.

wrong.A: The paragraph says illustrators are still hard at work.
wrong.C: The paragraph names books, magazines, and other places today.
wrong.D: The paragraph says they work closely with authors.

HIGH.stem: Why might a picture book page show only one single scene?
options: To save paper on each page
To make the book very short
To help young readers follow
To keep all the words hidden
HIGH.why: The article says one scene per page helps young readers see who is in the story, where it is, and what is happening.

wrong.A: The article does not mention saving paper.
wrong.B: The article does not say the book is short.
wrong.D: The pictures go with the words, they do not hide them.
